hints: Notice the horizontal forces along the $40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ velocity: $500 \text{ kN}$ engine thrust forward and $200 \text{ kN}$ air resistance backward, while $600 \text{ kN}$ lift and $600 \text{ kN}$ weight are vertical.
Recall that rate of change of kinetic energy equals net useful power, $P = Fv$, using the resultant force in the direction of motion, not thrust alone.
First subtract to get the resultant forward force in $\text{kN}$, convert to $\text{N}$, then multiply by $40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and convert $\text{W}$ to $\text{MW}$.
walkthrough: Identify forces in the direction of motion. Forward is $500 \text{ kN}$ engine thrust and backward is $200 \text{ kN}$ air resistance. Lift and weight are both $600 \text{ kN}$ and perpendicular to velocity, so they do no work and cancel.
Find the resultant forward force causing acceleration: $F_{net} = 500 \text{ kN} - 200 \text{ kN} = 300 \text{ kN} = 300 \times 10^3 \text{ N}$.
Use the power relation for a force parallel to velocity: $P = Fv$. The net power goes into increasing kinetic energy.
Substitute $F_{net} = 300 \times 10^3 \text{ N}$ and $v = 40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$: $P = 300 \times 10^3 \times 40 = 12 \times 10^6 \text{ W}$.
Convert to megawatts: $12 \times 10^6 \text{ W} = 12 \text{ MW}$. This is the rate of increase of kinetic energy. This is option C.

options.A: Too small for a $300 \text{ kN}$ resultant at $40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ - it does not equal resultant force times velocity.
options.B: This is $200 \times 10^3 \times 40 = 8.0 \text{ MW}$, the power lost working against air resistance only, not the net power.
options.C: Net forward force $300 \text{ kN}$ times $40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $12 \times 10^6 \text{ W} = 12 \text{ MW}$ increase in kinetic energy.
options.D: This is $500 \times 10^3 \times 40 = 20 \text{ MW}$, the engine thrust power only, ignoring the $200 \text{ kN}$ air resistance.
